claim: Ndt80 is a conserved transcription regulator across a large group of fungal species encompassing approximately 300 million years of diversity.
source: To address these questions, we examined the evolutionary history of Ndt80, a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein that is deeply conserved across a large group of fungal species encompassing approximately 300 million years of diversity.
evidence: The manuscript states this directly in the Introduction section.

claim: In most fungal species, Ndt80 controls meiosis and sporulation.
source: In most of these species, Ndt80 controls meiosis and sporulation, the coupled processes that form a portion of the fungal sexual cycle (Chu and Herskowitz, 1998; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chu and Herskowitz, 1998 and Xu et al., 1995.

claim: In the lineage leading to Candida albicans, Ndt80 acquired a new role as a master regulator of biofilm formation.
source: However, in the narrow lineage leading to the human fungal pathogen species Candida albicans, Ndt80 acquired a new role as a master regulator of the gene regulatory network that controls the formation of biofilms, multicellular communities of surface-associated cells (Figure 1A) (Nobile et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nobile et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Biofilms enable C. albicans to persist on mucosal surfaces and on implanted medical devices.
source: This newly evolved trait enables C. albicans to persist on mucosal surfaces and on implanted medical devices (Bonhomme and d'Enfert, 2013; Kojic and Darouiche, 2004; Nobile et al., 2012) and is responsible for many of the disease-causing properties of C. albicans (Nobile and Johnson, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonhomme and d'Enfert, 2013; Kojic and Darouiche, 2004; Nobile et al., 2012; and Nobile and Johnson, 2015.

claim: Ndt80 controls the expression of hundreds of genes involved in biofilm formation in C. albicans.
source: Ndt80 alone controls the expression of hundreds of genes involved in biofilm formation—but it appears to have evolved relatively recently (Nobile et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nobile et al., 2012.

claim: Ndt80's role changed from regulating sporulation and meiosis to regulating biofilm formation approximately 20 to 100 million years ago.
source: In this paper, we infer that approximately 20 to 100 million years ago (Taylor and Berbee, 2006), Ndt80's role changed from regulating sporulation and meiosis (its ancestral role) to regulating biofilm formation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor and Berbee, 2006 for the time estimate.

claim: The Ndt80 regulon was continuously undergoing significant rewiring in all lineages examined, even in those where the overall function of Ndt80 remained unchanged.
source: Instead, we found that the Ndt80 regulon was continuously undergoing significant rewiring in all lineages examined, even in those where the overall function of Ndt80 remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ChIP-Seq data across multiple species.

claim: The extent of Ndt80 rewiring was approximately the same whether its function had changed or not.
source: Indeed, at the resolution of our experiments, the extent of Ndt80 rewiring was approximately the same whether its function had changed or not.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on comparative analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The cis-regulatory motif bound by Ndt80 is highly conserved between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: Despite the significant differences in Ndt80 targets, however, the cis-regulatory sequence bound by Ndt80 in both species is highly conserved ([Jolly et al., 2005; Nobile et al., 2012], Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jolly et al., 2005 and Nobile et al., 2012, and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fewer than 13% of the targets of Ndt80 in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans are shared.
source: By all methods, fewer than 13% of the targets of Ndt80 in these two species are shared; with the most stringent criteria this drops to 3.4% (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: C. albicans has two paralogs of Ndt80 resulting from a gene duplication.
source: While the NDT80 genes in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans discussed above are homologous, C. albicans has an additional paralog of Ndt80, resulting from a gene duplication (Figure 2A, [Sellam et al., 2010]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sellam et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ndt80B is required for biofilm formation in C. albicans.
source: While Ndt80B has been shown to be required for biofilm formation in C. albicans (Nobile et al., 2012), the regulatory function of Ndt80A is unknown (deletion of Ndt80A has no effect on biofilm formation (Figure 4H, [Nobile et al., 2012]) or any other phenotype tested).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nobile et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The targets of Ndt80A represent a small subset (9-11%) of the targets of Ndt80B in C. albicans.
source: We found that the targets regulated by Ndt80A represent a small subset of the targets of Ndt80B (9–11%, Figure 1—figure supplement 3); that is, Ndt80A binds to many fewer genomic regions, but all these regions are also bound by Ndt80B.
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only ten genes are targets of Ndt80 in all five species tested (S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, P. pastoris, S. stipitis, and C. albicans).
source: Consistent with the idea that Ndt80 has acquired a unique set of targets in each species, only ten genes are targets of Ndt80 in all five species tested (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There are more Ndt80 targets bound in only one species (3261) than bound in two or more species.
source: This number pales in comparison to the 3261 genes that are Ndt80 targets in just one of the five species (Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The differences in Ndt80-target gene connections are predominantly determined by the distribution of cis-regulatory sequences across different genomes rather than changes in the Ndt80 protein itself.
source: These results demonstrate that changes in the Ndt80 protein sequence across species have had only a minor effect on the Ndt80-target gene connections; instead, the connections are predominantly determined by the distribution of cis-regulatory sequences across the different genomes.
evidence: Based on heterologous expression experiments comparing P. pastoris Ndt80 in S. cerevisiae vs. native Ndt80 in each species.

claim: Deletion of ndt80 in K. lactis results in complete deficiency in sporulation.
source: We first tested whether this deletion had an effect on sporulation and found, in K. lactis and P. pastoris, that the ndt80 deletion mutant is completely deficient in its ability to sporulate (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of ndt80 in P. pastoris results in complete deficiency in sporulation.
source: We first tested whether this deletion had an effect on sporulation and found, in K. lactis and P. pastoris, that the ndt80 deletion mutant is completely deficient in its ability to sporulate (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of Ndt80A in C. lusitaniae results in complete deficiency in sporulation.
source: Deletion of one paralog (Ndt80A) results in a complete deficiency in sporulation, while deletion of the other paralog (Ndt80B) results in a significant reduction in sporulation efficiency (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of Ndt80B in C. lusitaniae results in a significant reduction in sporulation efficiency.
source: Deletion of one paralog (Ndt80A) results in a complete deficiency in sporulation, while deletion of the other paralog (Ndt80B) results in a significant reduction in sporulation efficiency (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: C. albicans has never been observed to undergo sporulation and meiosis.
source: In contrast to these four species, C. albicans has never been observed to undergo sporulation and meiosis, relying instead on an alternate parasexual cycle (Bennett and Johnson, 2003; Butler et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett and Johnson, 2003 and Butler et al., 2009.

claim: In the ancestor of S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, P. pastoris, C. lusitaniae, and C. albicans, Ndt80 regulated sporulation.
source: Given that Ndt80 is required for sporulation in S. cerevisiae (Chu and Herskowitz, 1998; Xu et al., 1995), K. lactis, P. pastoris, and C. lusitaniae, and given the phylogenetic relationship between these species (Figure 2A), the most parsimonious model is that, in the ancestor of these species, Ndt80 regulated sporulation.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic inference from experimental data and citations to Chu and Herskowitz, 1998 and Xu et al., 1995.

claim: Deletion of NDT80B in C. albicans causes a severe defect in surface adherence and biofilm formation.
source: In C. albicans, biofilms consist of thick structures of different cell types (yeast-form and hyphae) that can form both in vitro and in vivo [Andes et al., 2004]). Deletion of NDT80B in C. albicans causes a severe defect in surface adherence and biofilm formation (Figure 4H).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4H and citation to Andes et al., 2004.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, P. pastoris, and C. lusitaniae, ndt80 mutants and wild-type are comparable in their ability to adhere to a solid surface.
source: In contrast, in S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, P. pastoris, and C. lusitaniae, the ndt80 mutants and wild-type are comparable in their ability to adhere to a solid surface (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figures 4D-G.

claim: Five of the ten genes that are Ndt80 targets in all five species tested (CLN2, CLG1, GLN1, GDH2, RPS7a) are strongly upregulated in biofilm formation.
source: Notably, five of these genes (CLN2, CLG1, GLN1, GDH2, RPS7a) are strongly upregulated in biofilm formation (Fox et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fox et al., 2015.

claim: Conservation of overall Ndt80 function does not correlate with increased conservation of Ndt80 targets.
source: If we take into account the different divergence times for each of these two-species comparisons (normalizing to the divergence time between S. cerevisiae and K. lactis), we still find that conservation of overall Ndt80 function does not correlate with increased conservation of Ndt80 targets (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The targets of Ndt80 change extensively even while Ndt80's conserved role in regulating sporulation is maintained.
source: Overall, these results show that the targets of Ndt80 change extensively, even while Ndt80's conserved role in regulating sporulation is maintained (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only 25 genes show sporulation-activation across S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, and P. pastoris.
source: Only 25 genes show sporulation-activation across S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, and P. pastoris, while 577 genes are activated uniquely in only one of the three species.
evidence: Based on gene expression data comparing sporulation vs. mitotic growth.

claim: 577 genes are activated during sporulation uniquely in only one of the three species (S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, P. pastoris).
source: Only 25 genes show sporulation-activation across S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, and P. pastoris, while 577 genes are activated uniquely in only one of the three species.
evidence: Based on gene expression data comparing sporulation vs. mitotic growth.

claim: Only seven genes show Ndt80-dependent expression in all three species (S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, P. pastoris).
source: We also measured global gene expression in an ndt80 deletion mutant in both K. lactis and P. pastoris under sporulation conditions, and found that the genes whose expression depends on Ndt80 during sporulation also differ significantly across species, with only seven genes showing Ndt80-dependent expression in all three species (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on gene expression data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transcription regulator Ndt80 underwent extensive rewiring of its regulatory connections before it became incorporated into a newly evolving regulatory network.
source: Using experiments performed in six different extant yeast species, we have deduced that the transcription regulator Ndt80 underwent extensive rewiring of its regulatory connections before it became incorporated into a newly evolving regulatory network.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on the combined experimental data from all species.

claim: The switch in Ndt80 function was not accompanied by a change in the DNA-binding specificity of Ndt80.
source: We have shown that this switch in function was not accompanied by a change in the DNA-binding specificity of Ndt80 (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4); rather, a change in the distribution of the conserved Ndt80 cis-regulatory sequence across hundreds of genes in the genome largely accounts for the different functions of Ndt80 in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
evidence: Based on motif analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A change in the distribution of the conserved Ndt80 cis-regulatory sequence across hundreds of genes in the genome largely accounts for the different functions of Ndt80 in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: We have shown that this switch in function was not accompanied by a change in the DNA-binding specificity of Ndt80 (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4); rather, a change in the distribution of the conserved Ndt80 cis-regulatory sequence across hundreds of genes in the genome largely accounts for the different functions of Ndt80 in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq and motif analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The inherent flexibility of the Ndt80 regulon facilitated the exploration of new regulatory networks.
source: We propose that the inherent flexibility of the Ndt80 regulon facilitated the exploration of new regulatory networks, allowing it to reach positions in 'network space' that allowed for the evolution of a novel phenotype.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data.

claim: Many different networks can orchestrate meiosis and sporulation.
source: These observations, taken together, indicate that there is no 'universal' solution to meiosis and sporulation in terms of both the genes required for this process and the regulatory network itself. Instead, many different networks can apparently orchestrate this ancient process.
evidence: Based on the observation of extensive differences in sporulation genes and networks across species.

claim: Continuous exploration of regulatory connections available to Ndt80 facilitated it reaching a network configuration that supported a new role in biofilm regulation.
source: We propose that the continuous exploration of regulatory connections available to Ndt80—while still maintaining its role in sporulation—facilitated it reaching a network configuration that supported a new role in biofilm regulation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data.

claim: Gene regulatory networks are inherently flexible, allowing for the exploration of many configurations that maintain an overall function.
source: Computational models had previously led to this view, namely that gene regulatory networks are inherently flexible, allowing for the exploration of many configurations that maintain an overall function (Barve and Wagner, 2013; Wagner, 2005a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barve and Wagner, 2013 and Wagner, 2005a.

claim: Continuous rewiring of gene regulatory networks predisposes regulators to a shift in function.
source: While much regulatory rewiring likely occurs through drift with no obvious shift in phenotype, we propose that continuous rewiring also predisposes regulators to a shift in function.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data.

claim: The heterologous P. pastoris Ndt80 does not complement the sporulation defect observed in an ndt80 deletion in S. cerevisiae.
source: These observations on the key role of cis-regulatory change do not mean that changes in the protein are unimportant; indeed, the heterologous P. pastoris Ndt80 does not complement the sporulation defect observed in an ndt80 deletion in S. cerevisiae (data not shown), nor does it occupy all the genome positions characteristic of the S. cerevisiae protein.
evidence: Based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: The heterologous P. pastoris Ndt80 protein occupies a substantial fraction of the S. cerevisiae-specific positions along the genome.
source: Our results do show, however, that the heterologous P. pastoris protein does occupy a substantial fraction of the S. cerevisiae-specific positions along the genome.
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data comparing heterologous P. pastoris Ndt80 in S. cerevisiae.

claim: The Ndt80 protein sequence differs considerably across the species tested, with only 55% similarity in the DNA-binding domain between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: The sequence of the Ndt80 protein does differ considerably across the species tested, with only 55% similarity in the DNA-binding domain between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans (Sellam et al., 2010), and 35% similarity in the proteins overall (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sellam et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is 35% similarity in the overall Ndt80 proteins between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: The sequence of the Ndt80 protein does differ considerably across the species tested, with only 55% similarity in the DNA-binding domain between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans (Sellam et al., 2010), and 35% similarity in the proteins overall (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on protein sequence comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A very large number of Ndt80 targets in K. lactis, P. pastoris, and S. stipitis are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans.
source: Counter to our initial expectation, we found that a very large number of Ndt80 targets in each species are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans (50% of all targets in K. lactis, 70% in P. pastoris, and 48% in S. stipitis, Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 50% of all Ndt80 targets in K. lactis are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans.
source: Counter to our initial expectation, we found that a very large number of Ndt80 targets in each species are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans (50% of all targets in K. lactis, 70% in P. pastoris, and 48% in S. stipitis, Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 70% of all Ndt80 targets in P. pastoris are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans.
source: Counter to our initial expectation, we found that a very large number of Ndt80 targets in each species are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans (50% of all targets in K. lactis, 70% in P. pastoris, and 48% in S. stipitis, Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 48% of all Ndt80 targets in S. stipitis are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans.
source: Counter to our initial expectation, we found that a very large number of Ndt80 targets in each species are not targets of Ndt80 in either S. cerevisiae or C. albicans (50% of all targets in K. lactis, 70% in P. pastoris, and 48% in S. stipitis, Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The protein Usv1 in S. cerevisiae has an ortholog in C. albicans called Bcr1, which is one of the master regulators of biofilm formation.
source: The protein Usv1 is particularly intriguing, as its ortholog in C. albicans, Bcr1, is one of the other master regulators of biofilm formation (Nobile et al., 2012; Nobile and Mitchell, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nobile et al., 2012 and Nobile and Mitchell, 2005.

claim: Two of the master regulators of biofilm formation, Ndt80 and Bcr1, may have had an ancestral regulatory relationship that was co-opted in the evolution of the biofilm regulatory network.
source: This observation suggests that two of the master regulators of biofilm formation, Ndt80 and Bcr1, may have had an ancestral regulatory relationship that was co-opted in the evolution of the biofilm regulatory network.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that Usv1/Bcr1 is a conserved Ndt80 target.

claim: In K. lactis and P. pastoris, Ndt80 is not expressed in mitotic cells.
source: Similarly, by performing transcription profiling, we find that in K. lactis and P. pastoris, Ndt80 is not expressed in mitotic cells (Supplementary file 1), consistent with the idea that Ndt80 is primarily needed during sporulation and is unlikely to have additional regulatory roles.
evidence: Based on transcription profiling data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Of the 65 genes known to be required for sporulation in S. cerevisiae that also exhibit sporulation-specific activation, only nine are activated during sporulation in both K. lactis and P. pastoris.
source: Of the 65 genes known to be required for sporulation in S. cerevisiae that also exhibit sporulation-specific activation, only nine are activated during sporulation in both K. lactis and P. pastoris, with 21 of these genes missing altogether from the genomes of one or both of these species (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: 21 of the 65 genes known to be required for sporulation in S. cerevisiae are missing altogether from the genomes of K. lactis or P. pastoris.
source: Of the 65 genes known to be required for sporulation in S. cerevisiae that also exhibit sporulation-specific activation, only nine are activated during sporulation in both K. lactis and P. pastoris, with 21 of these genes missing altogether from the genomes of one or both of these species (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Several key genes required for meiosis and sporulation in S. cerevisiae (IME1, ZIP2, SPO13) are missing from the genomes of species such as C. lusitaniae that are known to undergo meiosis and sporulation.
source: Consistent with this idea, it has previously been noted that several key genes required for meiosis and sporulation in S. cerevisiae (IME1, ZIP2, SPO13) are missing from the genomes of species such as C. lusitaniae that are known to undergo meiosis and sporulation (Bennett and Johnson, 2003; Sherwood and Bennett, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett and Johnson, 2003 and Sherwood and Bennett, 2009.

claim: Ndt80 gained a role in biofilm formation along the C. albicans lineage, after it branched off from C. lusitaniae.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Ndt80 regulated sporulation in the shared ancestor of S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, and that it gained a role in biofilm formation along the C. albicans lineage, after it branched off from C. lusitaniae (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rewiring of gene regulatory networks over evolutionary time is recognized as a key source of variation responsible for the modification of complex phenotypes.
source: Although the rewiring of gene regulatory networks over evolutionary time is recognized as a key source of variation responsible for the modification of complex phenotypes (Carroll, 2005; Davidson and Erwin, 2006; Li and Johnson, 2010; Wray, 2007), we still lack an understanding of how new, large gene regulatory networks controlling novel phenotypes arise over evolutionary time.
evidence: Supported by citations to Carroll, 2005; Davidson and Erwin, 2006; Li and Johnson, 2010; and Wray, 2007.

claim: It has been proposed that new gene regulatory networks arise from a combination of de novo genes as well as conserved genes that have undergone changes in regulation.
source: It has been proposed that new gene regulatory networks arise from a combination of de novo genes as well as conserved genes that have undergone changes in regulation (Wagner and Lynch, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wagner and Lynch, 2010.

claim: Transcription regulator-target gene interactions change over evolutionary timescales.
source: It has been well established that transcription regulator-target gene interactions change over evolutionary timescales.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The regulators controlling the ribosomal genes and the a-specific genes in fungi have changed over several hundred million years of evolution.
source: For example, the regulators controlling the ribosomal genes and the a-specific genes in fungi have changed over several hundred million years of evolution (Baker et al., 2012; Ihmels et al., 2005; Lavoie et al., 2010; Tanay et al., 2005; Tsong et al., 2006) (Sorrells et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker et al., 2012; Ihmels et al., 2005; Lavoie et al., 2010; Tanay et al., 2005; Tsong et al., 2006; and Sorrells et al., 2015.

claim: Transcription regulators such as Mcm1 and Ste12 have been shown to undergo extensive rewiring of their regulatory targets over evolutionary timescales.
source: Likewise, transcription regulators (such as Mcm1 and Ste12) have been shown to undergo extensive rewiring of their regulatory targets over similar timescales (Borneman et al., 2007; Tuch et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Borneman et al., 2007 and Tuch et al., 2008.

claim: Enhancers in Drosophila have been shown to undergo rapid changes in the nature and arrangement of their cis-regulatory sequences.
source: Such rewiring is not restricted to fungi; for example, enhancers in Drosophila have been shown to undergo rapid changes in the nature and arrangement of their cis-regulatory sequences (Frankel et al., 2012; Gompel et al., 2005; Ludwig et al., 2000; Swanson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frankel et al., 2012; Gompel et al., 2005; Ludwig et al., 2000; and Swanson et al., 2011.

claim: High degree of network plasticity seems to be a general feature of many regulatory networks.
source: This high degree of network plasticity seems to be a general feature of many regulatory networks.
evidence: This is stated as a general conclusion based on the cited literature.
